newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament steps up pressure on Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament steps up pressure on Yeltsin.

text.p: Russia's communist opposition stepped up pressure on President Boris Yeltsin over his health on Wednesday, saying he was unable to exercise power and the country was in deep crisis.

"We deputies cannot ignore the public's worry," Gennady Seleznyov, the communist chairman of the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament, said in a rallying cry at the start of a new parliamentary session.

Doctors said on Tuesday that Yeltsin's condition had improved considerably in the elite Moscow hospital where he is being treated for double pneumonia, but they did not say when he would be well enough to leave.
The presidential press service issued no news on the president's condition on Wednesday morning, but the chief Kremlin doctor was due to brief reporters within hours.

The Kremlin said Yeltsin, who turns 66 on February 1, was working on documents in hospital. Such reports often appear intended to show the president is able to tackle affairs of state and ease any concern over his health problems.
Seleznyov stepped up the opposition Communist Party's attacks on Yeltsin, one day after it started moves in parliament to look at ways to remove the president on health grounds.
The communists still have a large following among people disillusioned with reforms, but they were beaten by their old foe Yeltsin in a presidential election last year.
Seleznyov, one of the communists' most respected leaders, told the lower house that the powerful presidency was no longer functioning properly because of Yeltsin's poor health.
"Constitutional power has been concentrated in it (the presidency) and the president finds himself in a position of being unable to exercise it," he said.
"We are seeing a systemic crisis in the state, which is manifested in a crisis of authority."

He did not specifically call for Yeltsin to step down and made no comment on a motion put forward on Tuesday by fellow communist Viktor Ilyukhin calling on the State Duma lower house to look into ways to force Yeltsin out of office.
Seleznyov played down the chances of ousting Yeltsin in comments to reporters on Tuesday.
Yeltsin dismissed the need for constitution changes to limit his powers during talks with Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais on Tuesday.

The communists say Chubais has amassed power since the president suffered heart problems just before his re-election last July. Yeltsin had bypass surgery on November 5 and was away from his Kremlin office until December 23.

"In the president's absence individuals appear who try to run the state...in the president's name. This is always fraught with the danger of revolutions or plots, or massive intrigues in general," Ilyukhin told NTV commercial television.

Western leaders have reacted calmly to Yeltsin's latest illness. Some say Russia steered clear of major upheavals during his almost six-month absence from the Kremlin last year and that there is no reason why it should become more unstable now.
Yeltsin's political rivals say otherwise. Sacked security adviser Alexander Lebed, visiting Germany on Tuesday, said the country was in chaos and that he was the man to put it right.
Lebed would be a strong challenger if a presidential election were called early.
